extracted.intended_audience: students of literature, critics, and novelists (aspiring and established)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for the novel as a literary form — how to judge and how to write novels, covering story, characterization, plot, fantasy, prophecy, pattern, rhythm, point of view, and critical method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel defined
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A fiction in prose of a certain extent’ (une fiction en prose d’une certaine étendue); for the purposes of these lectures Forster adds that the extent should not be less than 50,000 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this working definition when deciding what counts as a novel for criticism or comparison; Forster notes this inclusively (it aims to include works such as The Pilgrim’s Progress, Ulysses, etc., unless strong reasons for exclusion are offered). Also: when he says 'English' he means 'written in English' (not geographically restricted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Story (the story-telling aspect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental aspect of the novel is its story-telling aspect: a novel ‘tells a story’ — this is the backbone (Forster likens it to a backbone or tape-worm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize story as necessary (readers often prize a good story), but not sufficient for literary greatness: it is ancient and atavistic; different readers value story differently (from indifferent to insistently story-first). Critically, avoid overvaluing mere sequence-of-events at the expense of other artistic aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: People (characterization): flat vs round characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes 'flat' characters (simple, built around a single idea and repeatable) from 'round' characters (complex, capable of surprising in a convincing way).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate characters by how much they can surprise the reader yet remain credible; round characters have inner life and development, flat characters are useful for certain effects or genres. Forster gives examples and emphasizes the 'novelist's touch' in drawing character. Consider how character-drawing techniques vary historically and stylistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (causal arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is the arrangement of events according to causation — distinct from mere story (sequence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how well events are tied by cause and consequence; plot is an artful ordering, producing necessity, surprise, coherence. Evaluate whether plot enhances or constrains character and theme rather than merely assembling incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy
rubrics_metrics.description: An aspect/technique in which writers (fantasists like Sterne or Virginia Woolf) treat reality by imaginative detours: starting from small objects, fluttering off in associations, combining muddle and beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the novel’s use of fantasy by its tone (deliberate bewilderment, associative leaps), how it balances humor/muddle with appreciation of beauty, and whether the technique sustains interest without collapsing into mere eccentricity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy
rubrics_metrics.description: A separate aspect Forster names: a novel’s prophetic power — the capacity to reveal truths about human life or to forecast/illuminate the future condition of humanity (Forster’s discussion indexed at 182–183).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether and how a novel transcends its subject-matter to make broader statements about human nature or future possibilities; consider whether such ‘prophecy’ is plausible, illuminating, or merely rhetorical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern (external form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern means the external shape or structure imposed on a novel (symmetries, designs, obvious motifs or banners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether an imposed external pattern creates beauty or becomes a sacrifice that readers find ‘not worth doing.’ Pattern can be ornamental but risks making the novel feel contrived; weigh pattern against the novel’s humanity and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm (internal repetition plus variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm in fiction—defined in the easy sense as 'repetition plus variation' and in a harder sense as a larger unifying rhythmic relation akin to a symphony’s unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for recurring motifs, phrases, or musical-like phrases (Forster’s Proust example: Vinteuil’s 'little phrase') that stitch the work from within. Good rhythm yields surprise and freshness; bad rhythm hardens into boring symbol and trips the reader. Large-scale rhythmic unity is rare but desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view (narrative perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice and control of narrative perspective (omniscient, limited, first person, authorial intrusions) and the technical usage of reporting speech ('he said'/'she said') which varies historically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate consistency and appropriateness of point of view, how the POV shapes reader sympathy and information, and whether shifts are justified. Forster notes that historical differences in reporting speech affect tone and must be taken into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone (personal vs impersonal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel’s tone can be broadly personal or impersonal (Chevalley’s two tones), and the effect depends on the author's genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess which tone the book adopts and whether it succeeds; note Forster’s caveat that 'genius' is often invoked but must be considered critically rather than as an escape from analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique and tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific technical devices (technique of conversation, methods of laughter, fantasy execution, use of 'he said') and their development form a literary tradition that changes over generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically attend to technique (how jokes are raised, how conversation is rendered, how fantasy is executed) as these affect effect and meaning. Comparing technique across works helps locate a novel within literary traditions/phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final test: human affection vs sentimentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster asserts that the final test of a novel will be our affection for it; the intensely human quality of a novel is unavoidable, but sentimentality (unreflective liking/disliking) is a danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance emotional response with critical judgment: affection is a legitimate test but must be guarded against unexamined sentimentality. Critics should avoid letting mere 'I like it' or 'I don't like it' be decisive without analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pseudo-scholarship and facile classification
rubrics_metrics.description: A methodological injunction for critics: do not substitute classifying books by date, locality, subject-matter, or gimmicky taxonomies (e.g., 'the literature of the weather') for reading and understanding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read books carefully instead of imposing chronological or topical categories; beware of classifying before comprehension. Forster gives many anti-pattern examples (classification by dates, 'tendencies', the nine kinds of weather) and condemns this as pernicious pseudo-scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid provincialism in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics must have a wide outlook and avoid patriotic/myopic judgments (Forster warns against denying foreign masterpieces such as Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Proust).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare works beyond national boundaries; a critic’s provincialism is a serious fault—novelists may be provincial without shame, but critics must not be. Place English fiction in the wider European/global context when warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: On the critic’s limitations: prefer aspects to chronology
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster advises critics (especially non-specialist 'pseudo-scholars') to analyze novels by aspects (story, people, plot, etc.) rather than by historical periods or influence-chains which require exhaustive knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When lacking exhaustive chronological scholarship, adopt the 'aspects' method: imagine novelists working side-by-side and analyze the various facets of their work. This is a prescriptive critical method rather than an aesthetic criterion for novels themselves.
